The problem

Ingest keeps growing. Nobody can say what is safe to cut.

Debug logging left on after an incident, a feed onboarded twice, sources for a project that ended last year. Each one adds to the bill, and without proof that nobody uses it, nobody wants to be the one who turns it off.

  • You pay by volume

    Your Splunk cost follows the GB/day you ingest, whether anyone searches it or not.

  • Usage is invisible

    License reports show what comes in. They don't show what anyone actually uses.

  • Evidence settles it

    "Zero searches, alerts or scheduled reports in 90 days" is a conversation the data owner can say yes to.

What you get

Every finding comes with its evidence.

The Pro report doesn't just list numbers. It explains in plain language why each dataset was flagged, so you can take it straight to the data owner.

Example from the sample report

app:debug_verbose POSSIBLE_WASTE
Ingest
38.0 GB/day
Searches in 90 days
0
Used by alerts
No
Scheduled reports
No

This dataset appears as a candidate because it ingests 38.0 GB/day, has no interactive searches in the last 90 days, and was not found in alerts or scheduled saved searches.

Recommendation: review the ingestion or filtering policy with the data owner.

What each label means

  • POSSIBLE_WASTE

    High volume and no searches, alerts or scheduled reports in 90 days. The strongest candidates.

  • REVIEW

    Some signs of low use, but not enough to be sure. Worth a check with the owner.

  • HIGH_VALUE

    Used by alerts, scheduled reports or frequent searches. Keep it.

  • PROTECTED

    Security, audit and compliance data. Never flagged as waste, whatever the numbers say.

  • NORMAL UNKNOWN

    Normal use, or not enough signal to classify. Shown so the inventory is complete.

Validation

Tested end to end against real Splunk Enterprise.

Before launch, the tool was run against a Splunk Enterprise 10.4.3 lab built for this purpose: real indexes with different volumes, real interactive searches, a real scheduled report and a real alert with an email action.

What has not been validated yet: Splunk Cloud, and production-scale volumes. If you run it there, I want to hear how it goes.

  • 7 out of 7 classifications correct

    Each lab dataset (frequent searches, scheduled-only, alert-only, protected, normal, review, unused) landed in the expected category.

  • Safe with restricted tokens

    With a role that cannot read _audit, the tool notices it and never reports data as unused. It downgrades the finding and tells you why.

  • Clean failures

    Invalid tokens, unreachable hosts and missing permissions produce a clear message, not a stack trace or a half-built report.

  • Real bugs fixed

    Running against real Splunk found three issues that synthetic data never would. All three are fixed and covered by regression tests.

Free, no download

Three Splunk searches to see where your ingest goes.

Paste these into Splunk Search today. They need the search capability and read access to _internal and _audit. No admin role.

  1. 1. Your biggest datasets, in GB/day

    index=_internal source=*license_usage.log type="Usage" earliest=-30d@d latest=@d
| stats sum(b) as bytes by idx, st
| eval gb_per_day=round(bytes/1024/1024/1024/30, 2)
| sort - gb_per_day
| head 20
| rename idx as index, st as sourcetype

  2. 2. Which indexes people actually search

    index=_audit action=search info=granted search=* earliest=-30d
NOT user=splunk-system-user
| rex field=search max_match=10 "index\s*=\s*\"?(?<searched_index>[\w\-\*]+)"
| mvexpand searched_index
| stats count as searches dc(user) as users by searched_index
| sort - searches

  3. 3. Sourcetypes that went quiet

    | metadata type=sourcetypes index=*
| eval days_since_last_event=round((now()-recentTime)/86400, 1)
| table sourcetype, totalCount, days_since_last_event
| sort - days_since_last_event

Anything big in list 1 that never shows up in list 2 is worth a conversation. Matching them by hand gets slow past a few dozen datasets, and searches that reach data through macros, eventtypes, alerts or scheduled reports are easy to miss. That cross-check is what the free Quickscan automates.

FAQ

Questions Splunk admins ask first.

Do I have to give the tool my Splunk credentials?

No. In CSV mode you run the bundled searches yourself, export the results and point the tool at the folder. It never talks to Splunk. REST mode is optional and uses a read-only token you provide, which stays on your machine.

What Splunk permissions does it need?

The search capability plus read access to _internal (license usage) and _audit (search activity). No admin role. It never creates, modifies or deletes configuration or data.

Why does the free download go through a checkout?

Community is delivered through Lemon Squeezy so you get a permanent download link by email. It costs nothing and needs no license key.

I'm on a Mac or Windows laptop. Can I use it?

The current build runs on Linux x86_64 with glibc 2.35 or newer, for example a jump host, a VM or WSL2 with Ubuntu 22.04. Native macOS and Windows builds come later.

Will it tell me to delete data?

No. It classifies each index and sourcetype and shows the evidence behind it. Findings are candidates to review with the data owner; savings are an estimate, not a guarantee, and you decide what to change.

What do I get with Pro that Quickscan doesn't show?

The classification of every dataset, the evidence and explanation for each one, the Data Value Score, recommendations, risks and methodology, as an HTML and Markdown report you can share. Here is a complete example.

What if Pro doesn't work for my environment?

Write to support@logspendauditor.com within 14 days of purchase and you get a full refund. Purchases are processed by Lemon Squeezy, so the refund goes back to the same payment method.
